Leinster
LEN-stur
n. (the eastern Irish province of Dublin, where Trinity College was founded in 1592 and the Irish New Testament printed in 1602)
From Irish Laighin, the name of the eastern people, with the Norse staðr, a place, giving the English form.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Leinster is the eastern Irish province, with Dublin at its centre and the Pale about it, and it is where Irish Protestantism did its scholarly work. Trinity College Dublin was founded in 1592 as a seminary for a Protestant ministry; James Ussher entered it as one of its first students, became its professor of divinity and then Archbishop of Armagh, and built the library whose catalogue of Hebrew, Greek and patristic texts was the best in Ireland. The Irish Articles of 1615, drafted largely by Ussher and adopted by the Irish convocation, are more explicitly Calvinist than the Thirty-nine, affirming predestination, reprobation and the perseverance of the saints in terms the English articles leave open. Dublin was also where the Scriptures were put into Irish: William Daniel's Irish New Testament was printed there in 1602 and the Book of Common Prayer in Irish in 1608, and William Bedell, Bishop of Kilmore, had the Old Testament translated by 1640, though it was not printed until 1685. The dictionary records the college, the articles and the Irish Bible together, and holds the third the most important of the three.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a college as a society of men for literary purposes; convocation as an assembly of the clergy; an article as a clause of a confession; a version as a translation; and to prepare as to make ready.

expand to see more

COLLEGE, n. A collection or society of men, invested with certain powers, and engaged in some common pursuit, especially literary.

CONVOCATION, n. An assembly; in England, an assembly of the clergy, by their representatives, to consult on ecclesiastical affairs.

ARTICLE, n. A single clause or item of an account, a confession or a charge; a distinct proposition.

VERSION, n. A translation; the act of rendering into another language; as the common version of the Scriptures.

PREPARE, v.t. To fit, adapt or qualify for a particular purpose; to make ready; to provide.

Key Scripture

Act 2:8 — "And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?"

1Co 14:19 — "Yet in the church I had rather speak five words with my understanding, that by my voice I might teach others also, than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue."

Neh 8:8 — "So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading."

Ezr 7:10 — "For Ezra had prepared his heart to seek the law of the LORD, and to do it, and to teach in Israel statutes and judgments."

Modern Corruption

Eastern Irish province of Dublin and the Pale, where Trinity College was founded in 1592, the Calvinist Irish Articles adopted in 1615, and the Irish New Testament printed in 1602 and the whole Bible by 1685.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one the Irish Bible embodies and the one Irish Protestantism most often forgot: that a church sent to a people must speak to them in their own tongue, and that everything else it does is secondary to this. Daniel's New Testament of 1602 and Bedell's Old Testament were the right work. Pentecost is the standard, where the astonishment was that men heard “how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born” (Act 2:8), and Paul's own preference is for a few intelligible words over a quantity of unintelligible ones: “in the church I had rather speak five words with my understanding, that by my voice I might teach others also, than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue” (1Co 14:19).

The second thing to recover is the order of a scholar's work, which Ussher at his best exemplified and which his successors did not keep. Ezra's sequence is study, obedience, teaching, and in that order: “For Ezra had prepared his heart to seek the law of the LORD, and to do it, and to teach in Israel statutes and judgments” (Ezr 7:10). A college founded to supply a ministry and a convocation that adopted a Calvinist confession were doing the right things; what the establishment largely failed to do was the plainest thing of all, which is to read and open the text to the people in front of it, as at the reading of the law when they “gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8). Bedell's Old Testament sat in manuscript for forty-five years before anyone printed it, and the dictionary records that delay as the truest measure of how much the Irish establishment wanted the Irish to read.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek dialektos (G1258), a tongue; Greek nous (G3563), the understanding; Hebrew darash (H1875), to seek or study.

expand to see more

Greek dialektos (G1258) — a language, the speech of a people; “how hear we every man in our own tongue”, Acts 2:8.

Greek nous (G3563) — the mind, the understanding; “speak five words with my understanding”, 1 Corinthians 14:19.

Greek glossa (G1100) — the tongue, a language; “than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue”, 1 Corinthians 14:19.

Hebrew darash (H1875) — to seek, to enquire, to study; “prepared his heart to seek the law of the LORD”, Ezra 7:10.

Hebrew lamad (H3925) — to learn, to teach; “and to teach in Israel statutes and judgments”, Ezra 7:10.

Usage

"“how hear we every man in our own tongue” (Act 2:8) — the Irish New Testament printed at Dublin, 1602."

"“to seek the law of the LORD, and to do it, and to teach” (Ezr 7:10) — Ussher's order at its best."

"“gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8) — Bedell's Old Testament unprinted for forty-five years."
